question: Your forehand is significantly better than your backhand. The opponent figures this out and feeds your backhand every ball. What's the right tactical adjustment?
option_a: Improve your backhand — it's the only honest answer
option_b: Structure the rally so you hit forehands from the backhand side — slide around, take it as an inside-out forehand whenever possible
option_d: Come to net on the next short ball regardless of position
why_right: When a weapon-and-weakness asymmetry exists, the answer is rarely 'fix the weakness mid-match' — it's 'set up the weapon despite the feed.' Sliding around to take backhand-side balls as inside-out forehands restores the asymmetry on your terms. The opponent is feeding what they think is your weakness; you're using their feed to construct your strength.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro built his entire baseline game around the principle that the forehand was the weapon and the backhand was the setup. His footwork was specifically designed to move him laterally to convert as many backhand-side balls as possible into inside-out forehands. The asymmetry was managed by movement, not by trying to make the backhand into something it wasn't.
common_pitfall: Trying to win backhand rallies on the day — fix the weakness off-court, work around it on-court.
action_tip: If your forehand is your weapon: structure your footwork to take as many balls as possible as inside-out forehands.
share_prompt: Do you fix your weakness — or amplify your weapon?

question: You're stretched wide on your forehand side and the opponent expects a crosscourt reply. You actually have time to set your feet. What's the highest-value choice?
option_a: Hit the expected crosscourt — never gift them a winner
option_b: Redirect down the line into the open court — the conditions briefly support the change
option_c: Slice short to throw them off
option_d: Loop a defensive ball deep and reset
why_right: Defensive position with set feet is not the same as defensive position with scrambling feet. When you have time to set up, the wide-court redirect becomes available — and your opponent is positioned for the expected crosscourt, leaving the down-the-line lane open. The window is narrow but it's real. The condition that makes it work is set feet, not the wide position alone.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's signature defensive-position forehand was the redirect — not the safe crosscourt absorption. When he had time to set feet from a wide position, he turned defense into offense by redirecting into the open court behind the opponent. The opponent was reading crosscourt because the position said crosscourt; the redirect existed only because del Potro's setup time made it possible.
common_pitfall: Always hitting crosscourt from wide positions because 'wide = defensive' — missing the moments when set feet make the redirect available.
action_tip: From wide forehand position with set feet: scan for the down-the-line redirect before defaulting to the safe crosscourt.

question: You see a weak second serve coming. You want to take control of the point with the first ball back. What's the right target?
option_a: Drive flat through the middle to limit their angle
option_b: Crosscourt to your strong side — pull them off the court and set up your next ball
option_c: Drop shot — they're rooted at the baseline
option_d: Down the line to surprise them
why_right: The first ball off a weak second serve is the highest-leverage attacking ball of the point. The target is not a winner attempt — it's setting up the second shot. Pulling the opponent off the court with a crosscourt drive opens space for the next ball to attack into. Flat through the middle limits their angle but also limits yours. The first ball builds; the second ball finishes.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's return-to-attack pattern off weak second serves was a crosscourt forehand to pull the opponent wide, followed by an inside-out forehand into the open space. The return itself was rarely the winner — it was the construction of the next-ball attack. The serve gave him the first ball; the first ball gave him the second.
common_pitfall: Trying to win the point with the return itself — and missing the next-ball attack the right return would have set up.
action_tip: On a weak second-serve return: hit crosscourt to your strong side to set up the next ball — the second shot is the finisher.
share_prompt: Is the return the winner — or the setup?

question: You're three sets into a long match, physically tired, and you can feel your decision-making degrading. Your B-side patterns are missing more than usual. What's the right adjustment?
option_a: Take more risks to end points faster
option_b: Restrict yourself almost entirely to your A-side weapon — even if it means longer setups
option_c: Push through with your full pattern set — the fatigue is in your head
option_d: Slow down between every point to recover
why_right: Fatigue does not erase your weapon — it erases your supporting shots first. The discipline under physical strain is to narrow the game to the weapon and accept that points may take longer to construct. Continuing to play eight patterns when only two are still executing reliably means six of every ten balls are below threshold. Better to play two patterns well than eight patterns badly.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's career was repeatedly interrupted by wrist injuries that demanded a tactical adjustment to physical reality. When he returned and could not always execute the full repertoire, his game narrowed deliberately to the forehand weapon. The simplification was not surrender — it was the recognition that the weapon survived the constraints that the surrounding game did not.
common_pitfall: Pushing through fatigue by trying harder with the same patterns — and missing the only honest adjustment, which is fewer patterns.
action_tip: When you notice fatigue degrading your B-side shots: simplify the game to your weapon. Construct the point around it for as long as it takes.
share_prompt: When fatigued, do you push harder — or narrow tighter?

question: Your forehand is your strongest shot. You want to design serve patterns that maximise the chance of getting a forehand on the next ball. What's the highest-value first-serve target from the deuce court?
option_a: Wide — it pulls them off court but their reply is usually a backhand to your backhand
option_b: T — it elicits a return to the middle, which you can step around and take as a forehand
option_c: Body — it jams them and produces a weak reply you can take with either side
option_d: All three equally — variety matters more than pattern
why_right: When your forehand is the weapon, the serve location should maximise the probability that the next ball is a forehand. A T-serve in the deuce court tends to produce a return down the centre line — which you can step around and take as an inside-in or inside-out forehand. A wide serve produces a return back to your backhand. Body serves vary too much. The pattern is built backward from the second ball.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's deuce-court serve patterns were heavily weighted toward the T because of the next-ball geometry: a T-serve produced a central return he could step around as an inside-out forehand into the open court. The first-serve target was chosen by the second shot it set up, not by the ace probability of the serve itself.
common_pitfall: Choosing serve targets for the ace probability instead of the next-ball geometry.
action_tip: If your forehand is your weapon: from deuce court, serve T more often — it gives you a central return you can convert into a forehand.
share_prompt: Do you serve for the ace — or for the next-ball forehand?

question: You're standing in the centre of the court with a ball arriving to your forehand. You can hit it inside-out or inside-in. What decides the choice?
option_c: Inside-out when their court geometry asks for it — long crosscourt diagonal to their weaker wing. Inside-in when they have leaked off-centre toward the other side
option_d: Pick whichever feels better in the moment
why_right: Inside-out and inside-in are not preferences — they are answers to different court conditions. Inside-out exploits the long crosscourt diagonal to the opponent's weaker side; inside-in exploits the opponent having drifted off-centre and the down-the-line lane being open. The wrong shot in the right condition is a missed opportunity; the right shot in the wrong condition is a gift. The court geometry decides.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's inside-out and inside-in forehands were both signature shots — but he chose between them by reading the opponent's court position, not by personal preference. Inside-out when the opponent's footwork showed they were anchored to one side; inside-in when their recovery had drifted past the centre. The shot followed the condition.
common_pitfall: Defaulting to inside-out because it's the safer of the two — and missing the inside-in when the opponent's drift makes it the obvious shot.
action_tip: Before stepping around to hit a forehand: read where their recovery position has drifted. The drift tells you inside-out or inside-in.
share_prompt: Do you pick the shot — or does the court pick it?

question: Your backhand is technically limited — you cannot redirect or attack with it consistently. The opponent has noticed. What is the right tactical role for your backhand?
option_a: Reduce its use as much as possible by running around
option_b: Use it as a depth-and-direction tool that holds the rally and lets you reset to neutral, never as a finisher
option_c: Slice every backhand short to disrupt rhythm
option_d: Add topspin and try to make it attacking
why_right: A limited backhand can still be a useful shot — provided you understand what it can and cannot do. Used as a depth-and-direction tool, it holds the rally, controls distance, and resets to neutral so you can construct the next point around your weapon. Trying to make it attacking when the technique doesn't support attack produces unforced errors. The shot has a job; the job is not to win the point.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's backhand was widely understood — by him and by his opponents — as the setup, not the finisher. He used it to hold rallies, control depth, and engineer the next ball into his forehand. The shot's value was in what it allowed him to do next, not in what it did itself. Treating a limited shot as limited is honest tactics, not surrender.
common_pitfall: Trying to upgrade your backhand mid-match — fix the technique off-court, deploy the shot honestly on-court.
action_tip: If your backhand is technically limited: deep, controlled, neutral — set up the next ball with it, don't try to win the point with it.
share_prompt: Does every shot have to win the point?

question: You're playing your first competitive match back from a significant injury. You can feel that some of your patterns aren't quite there yet. What's the right mindset?
option_a: Push through and trust the patterns will return mid-match
option_b: Restrict your tactical menu to patterns you can still execute reliably — accept that the full game is a future-tense reality, not a present-tense one
option_d: Play differently from your usual style to avoid putting stress on the recovery
why_right: Returning from injury, the patterns that survive are the ones you can execute. Trying to play your full pre-injury repertoire when half of it isn't there yet produces a degraded match performance and risks the recovery. The tactical answer is to restrict the menu honestly: play only what you can execute reliably, and treat the return of the rest as something that arrives over weeks of matches, not in this one.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's return matches after each of his wrist surgeries were studies in tactical honesty. He returned without the full pattern set he had before, and his game narrowed accordingly — leaning on what survived the recovery rather than forcing what didn't. The tactical patience was as important as the physical patience.
common_pitfall: Pretending the recovery is complete and playing your full pre-injury repertoire on the first match back — and either underperforming or re-injuring.
action_tip: First match back from injury: name the patterns you can still execute reliably. Play only those, for the whole match. The rest is for next month.
share_prompt: Returning from injury: is your game back — or just your body?

question: Your first serve is genuinely a weapon — top-of-your-game it hits 130mph with placement. What's the highest-value serve plan?
option_a: Maximum pace down the T every first serve
option_b: A locked-in pattern: same serve to the same spot until they prove they can return it consistently
option_c: Maximum variety — keep them guessing every point
option_d: Pick whichever serve feels strongest in the moment
why_right: A genuine weapon serve doesn't need variety to be effective — repetition is the weapon. Until the returner proves they can handle a specific serve consistently, that serve continues. Variety becomes valuable only after the returner has solved your default; before that, switching is a gift. The pattern is locked until it's broken.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro's first serve at the peak of his game leaned on locked-in patterns rather than randomised variety. The serve was good enough that the returner had to prove they could solve it before he moved on to a different pattern. Switching too early gave the returner relief; sticking with a pattern that was working compounded its value.
common_pitfall: Switching your serve pattern because the returner returned one — give them three before you change.
action_tip: If your serve is a weapon: lock the pattern until they return it consistently. Variety is the response to being read, not the default.

question: You're a counterpuncher with a single signature weapon (forehand). The opponent has been pushing you around but suddenly gives you a slightly shorter ball, well within your forehand strike zone. What's the right read?
option_a: Defend again — they may be baiting you with a sucker ball
option_b: Commit fully to the forehand — the trigger ball for a weapon-based counterpuncher is shorter, more central, and in the strike zone. This is it.
option_c: Drop shot — they're not expecting it
why_right: A counterpuncher who carries one signature weapon must have a tight definition of the trigger ball — the ball that justifies the full commitment to the weapon. The criteria are simple: shorter than usual, more central than usual, in the strike zone. When all three are met, the weapon must come out fully. Hesitation here is a missed point and, often, a missed match. The weapon is the difference between defending and winning; the trigger ball is the difference between counterpunching and just absorbing.
pro_insight: Juan Martin del Potro as a counterpuncher with a single weapon developed a tight, almost surgical definition of his trigger ball — short enough, central enough, in the strike zone. When the ball met those criteria, the forehand came out fully and unhesitatingly. The discipline was not in the swing; it was in the read of the ball that authorised it.
common_pitfall: Counterpunching too long — staying defensive on a ball that authorised the weapon, and giving back the point you'd already earned.
action_tip: If you're a counterpuncher with one weapon: define the trigger ball before the match — short, central, strike zone. When it arrives, commit fully.
